channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: Translation and Cross-Cultural Adaptation of the World Health Organization's Thinking Healthy Program into Persian for Implementation by Community Health Volunteers (Peers) in Iran's Health System.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study translated and culturally adapted the WHO’s Thinking Healthy Program (THP) for prenatal depression into Persian for delivery by community health volunteers (peers) in Iran, assessing feasibility and acceptability rather than clinical effectiveness.
FINDINGS: Seven pregnant women with EPDS ≥13 and five peers piloted the adapted THP. Key adaptations included culturally sensitive language, visuals, a sexual health module, and training on natural childbirth. Acceptability was high: 85.7% of mothers found the program comprehensible, and all peers endorsed feasibility.
INTERPRETATION: This is a small, uncontrolled pilot study focused on translation and feasibility, not efficacy. Strengths include systematic cultural adaptation using expert panels and qualitative feedback, but the sample is tiny and lacks a comparator or outcome data on depression reduction. Findings suggest acceptability but cannot establish effectiveness.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The adapted THP may be culturally acceptable for peer delivery in Iran, but routine use should await results from larger randomized trials evaluating clinical outcomes before recommending implementation in practice.

item.title: Low-threshold secondary and tertiary suicide prevention measures for individuals with suicid-related thoughts and behaviors: a scoping review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review examined low-threshold secondary and tertiary suicide prevention measures for adults with suicide-related thoughts and behaviors (STBs), excluding primary care, psychotherapy, pharmacotherapy, gatekeepers, and means restriction. The goal was to inform Germany’s 2024 National Suicide Prevention Strategy by synthesizing evidence on accessible interventions.
FINDINGS: Of 1,897 records, 24 studies were included. Voice-based (n=9) and text-based (n=7) crisis interventions (e.g., helplines) consistently reduced suicidal ideation and psychological distress, except one moderated peer-to-peer forum. Outreach messages (n=3) and web-based educational/counseling measures (n=5) showed heterogeneous but promising results. Most evidence pertained to short-term outcomes.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by heterogeneity, lack of RCTs, and short follow-up durations. Voice- and text-based interventions have the strongest support, but mechanisms and long-term effects remain unclear. The review highlights gaps in high-quality trials and calls for standardized outcome measures to strengthen conclusions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings support the use of voice/text crisis interventions in low-threshold settings, but clinicians should remain cautious about extrapolating benefits to long-term outcomes. More rigorous research is needed before widespread adoption of outreach or web-based measures.

item.title: Transdiagnostic Reductions in Glymphatic-Related Perivascular Diffusion Across Psychiatric Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examines whether glymphatic system dysfunction, measured by diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS), is a transdiagnostic feature across psychiatric disorders. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 32 studies (24 included in meta-analysis) compared DTI-ALPS indices between psychiatric patients (n=1,503) and healthy controls (n=1,352).
FINDINGS: The pooled random-effects meta-analysis found a significant reduction in DTI-ALPS index in psychiatric patients versus controls (Hedges' g = -0.78, 95% CI -1.01 to -0.55, p < 0.0001). Heterogeneity was substantial (I² = 86.3%), and small-study effects were detected.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests a robust but heterogeneous association between psychiatric disorders and reduced DTI-ALPS, indicating potential transdiagnostic glymphatic dysfunction. However, high heterogeneity and small-study effects limit certainty. The biological and clinical significance of DTI-ALPS reductions remains unclear, warranting harmonised imaging protocols and further validation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Currently, DTI-ALPS is not a validated or clinically actionable biomarker in psychiatry. Findings highlight a potential research direction but do not yet inform patient care or diagnostic decisions.

item.title: Screen time and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether excessive screen time in children is associated with increased risk of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), including potential moderating effects of age and media type. Ten observational studies with low-to-moderate risk of bias were synthesized using a random-effects model.
FINDINGS: The pooled analysis found a significant association between excessive screen time and ADHD risk (pooled OR = 1.56, 95% CI: 1.31–1.87, P < 0.001). Between-study heterogeneity was very high (I² = 97.4%). Subgroup analysis showed a stronger association in preschoolers (0–6 years: OR = 2.40, 95% CI: 1.44–3.98) than in older children (OR = 1.16, 95% CI: 1.05–1.29). Passive screen exposure (e.g., TV/video) showed a higher point estimate (OR ≈ 2.20) than interactive media (OR ≈ 1.10), though the difference was not statistically significant.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests a modest but statistically significant association between excessive early childhood screen time and ADHD risk, with the strongest signal in preschoolers and for passive media. However, the very high heterogeneity and observational nature of included studies limit causal inference. Residual confounding (e.g., parenting style, socioeconomic factors) and exposure misclassification may influence results. The lack of significant difference between media types should be interpreted cautiously due to limited power and variability in exposure definitions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence supports advising parents to limit screen exposure—especially passive, fast-paced content—in early childhood, while acknowledging that the observed effect is small and causality is not proven. Clinicians should counsel families on balanced screen use as part of general developmental guidance, without overstating ADHD risk as definitive.

item.title: Patient Navigation Plus mHealth Incentives for Linkage to OUD Care for Adults Who Also Use Methamphetamines: A Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This single-site pilot randomized clinical trial (RCT) tested whether a mobile health (mHealth) intervention with financial incentives and patient navigation (MIAPP) could improve linkage to outpatient buprenorphine care after hospitalization for opioid use disorder (OUD) among adults who also used methamphetamine. The study assessed feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary clinical outcomes in a US urban safety-net hospital.
FINDINGS: The trial enrolled 40 participants (mean age 43.4 years; 82.5% male). The intervention was delivered to 19 of 20 randomized participants. Patient satisfaction with the navigator was high (mean score 9.9/10). Linkage to OUD care within 30 days occurred in 11/20 (55.0%) in the MIAPP arm versus 10/20 (50.0%) in treatment-as-usual (TAU), with a risk ratio of 1.10 (95% CI 0.61–1.99). No significant between-group differences were observed for retention or readmissions at 90 days.
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates feasibility and high acceptability of the MIAPP intervention, but it is underpowered to detect meaningful differences in linkage or retention. The wide confidence interval around the risk ratio and lack of effect on secondary outcomes suggest that any true benefit, if present, is likely modest. Larger trials with longer follow-up and more diverse populations are needed to determine effectiveness and generalizability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, there is insufficient evidence to recommend MIAPP over standard care for improving linkage to buprenorphine treatment in hospitalized patients with OUD and methamphetamine use. Clinicians should continue to use established strategies to support post-discharge engagement while awaiting results from adequately powered trials.

item.title: Application of operant demand in autism and developmental disabilities: An updated review (2017-2025).
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The review asks whether operant demand analysis—from behavioral economics—has been increasingly and rigorously applied to individuals with autism and related developmental disabilities since 2017, and whether this framework is now used to assess treatment durability, schedule thinning, and generalization. It updates an earlier review and follows PRISMA guidelines.
FINDINGS: Thirty articles (31 experiments; n=307 participants) were identified. Use of demand and work-output analyses and unit-price applications increased, but open versus closed economies were rarely evaluated. There was substantial procedural variability in how “price” was manipulated, and generalization variables remained underused.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is growing but methodologically heterogeneous; effect sizes cannot be pooled because the review is descriptive. The rarity of open/closed economy comparisons and the variability in price manipulations limit firm conclusions about efficacy or durability. The lack of generalization-focused studies is a notable gap.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Operant demand analysis may be entering routine behavioral programming for schedule thinning and durability checks, but current evidence does not yet justify wholesale changes in practice; clinicians should scrutinize the specific economic arrangements used in individual programs.

item.title: Culinary-Medicinal Lion's Mane Mushroom Hericium erinaceus (Agaricomycetes) Mycelium Mitigates Ketamine Abuse Potential.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether *Hericium erinaceus* (Lion’s Mane) mycelium or its bioactive compound erinacine A could reduce ketamine’s abuse potential in a rat model of self-administration, addressing concerns about recreational ketamine use despite its therapeutic benefits.
FINDINGS: In male Sprague-Dawley rats trained to self-administer ketamine (0.5 mg/kg/infusion) or sucrose, higher doses of *H. erinaceus* mycelium significantly reduced ketamine intake and motivation under both fixed-ratio (FR2) and progressive-ratio (PR) schedules. Erinacine A also reduced ketamine intake but additionally decreased food reinforcement, whereas the mycelium did not affect sucrose or food intake.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preclinical (rat model) with clear dose-dependent effects on ketamine reinforcement, suggesting potential specificity for ketamine’s abuse liability. However, the reduction in food reinforcement with erinacine A raises concerns about broader motivational blunting. The study lacks human data, and the mechanism (e.g., neuropharmacology) is not explored. The findings are promising but preliminary, with uncertain generalisability to clinical settings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study does not yet justify clinical use of *H. erinaceus* or erinacine A to mitigate ketamine abuse in humans. Further research—including safety, tolerability, and efficacy in humans—is needed before any bedside application.

item.title: Perinatal insults, genetic susceptibility, and the pathogenesis of neurodevelopmental disorders: from epigenetic remodeling to neural circuit dysfunction-a narrative review.
item.description: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs)-including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), intellectual disability (ID), epilepsy, and schizophrenia-affect approximately 10-15% of children worldwide. Emerging evidence suggests that NDDs arise from complex interactions between genetic susceptibility and environmental insults, particularly during perinatal periods.

item.title: Bridging the gap between guidelines and practice: Outcomes of the BREF psychoeducational program for caregivers in psychiatry.
item.description: OBJECTIVES: Despite guidelines recommending early and systematic provision of family psychoeducation to caregivers of individuals with a severe mental disorder, such programs remain underutilized and infrequently implemented in mental health care settings. The BREF program was developed to enable early, systematic and sustainable support for caregivers in psychiatry. This study evaluated caregiver outcomes associated with participation in the BREF program using a single-group pre-post design.

item.title: Neural Circuits of Social Behavior in Autism Spectrum Disorder: From Mechanism to Intervention.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Difficulties in social communication and interaction are core diagnostic features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet interventions targeting these difficulties have modest and variable effects. Understanding mechanistically distinct contributions to social behaviors may identify new therapeutic opportunities. METHODS: This narrative review integrates human neuroimaging studies, supporting rodent circuit neuroscience, clinical intervention research, and developmental studies.

item.title: Genetic architecture and risk of suicide attempt across neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Suicide attempt (SA) is prevalent among individuals with neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions, yet similarities and differences in the genetic architecture of SA across these conditions remain unclear. METHODS: In the iPSYCH cohort (N=98,069), SA was identified using ICD-10 codes among individuals diagnosed with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (N=22,962), autism (N=17,670), schizophrenia (N=5,974), bipolar disorder (N=3,028), depression (N=28,844), and controls (N=34,049).

item.title: Probable alcohol use disorder in the U.S. Veteran population: Results from the 2025-2026 National Health and Resilience in Veterans study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a pervasive public health problem in the United States, and military veterans are at elevated risk. A prior wave of the National Health and Resilience in Veterans Study (NHRVS) estimated the prevalence of past-year probable AUD at 10.5 % in 2019-2020. Updated national surveillance data are needed given demographic shifts in the veteran population and evolving drinking patterns in the post-pandemic era.

item.title: Emerging information technologies across the autism service and prevention continuum: a narrative review of screening, diagnosis, intervention, and health equity.
item.description: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a major global public-health concern, yet timely identification and support remain difficult to access for many families, especially in rural, low-resource, and otherwise underserved settings. Emerging information technologies have been proposed as tools for narrowing this service gap. These include artificial intelligence (AI), wearable sensors, and the Internet of Things, mobile health applications and digital therapeutics, telehealth, immersive virtual and augmented reality, social robotics, and large language models.

item.title: Risk of Sexually Transmitted Infections Among Pregnant Persons With Substance Use Diagnoses.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in pregnancy have increased among reproductive-aged women and are associated with adverse maternal and infant outcomes. Identifying high-risk groups for perinatal STIs, including those with differential substance use diagnoses, is essential. This study examines the risk of STIs in pregnancy by specific isolated and co-occurring substance use diagnoses. METHODS: Data stem from a population-based study of pregnant individuals with liveborn, singleton deliveries in California from 2011 to 2021.

item.title: Structure-based discovery of a novel Granzyme A (GZMA) inhibitor for autism spectrum disorder through integrative transcriptomics, virtual screening, and long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations.
item.description: Granzyme A (GZMA) is a trypsin-like serine protease expressed in cytotoxic lymphocytes that cleaves gasdermin B (GSDMB) to release a pore-forming N-terminal fragment, thereby inducing pyroptosis, a lytic and pro-inflammatory form of programmed cell death. This pathway has been implicated in immune dysregulation reported in a subset of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

item.title: Urban-Rural and Demographic Differences in Substance Use Among High School Students - Youth Risk Behavior Survey, United States, 2025.
item.description: Adolescent substance use remains a critical public health concern. Understanding patterns of substance use might guide prevention strategies and identify populations in need of focused, tailored interventions. This report links nationally representative 2025 Youth Risk Behavior Survey data with school characteristics data to describe substance use behaviors and differences by demographic characteristics and among students in public schools for whom locale information was available, by urban-rural classification.

item.title: Prevalence of Binge Eating Behavior Among High School Students and Associations with Social Media Use, Mental Health, and Suicide Risk - Youth Risk Behavior Survey, United States, 2025.
item.description: Disordered eating among adolescents is a public health concern, and binge eating, which is eating an unusually large amount of food while feeling a loss of control, is among the most prevalent forms. In 2025, for the first time, the nationally representative Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) included an item assessing binge eating among U.S. high school students.

item.title: Barriers and facilitators to using an app-based tool for suicide safety planning in a psychiatric emergency department: A qualitative descriptive study using the Theoretical Domains Framework and COM-B model.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Emergency departments (EDs) play a crucial role in suicide prevention, with evidenced-based safety planning interventions (SPI) playing an important role. Traditional safety plans, which are often paper based, come with challenges (i.e., not easily accessible, or easy to misplace). Digital safety planning tools offer an alternative mode of intervention delivery, but clinical implementation remains limited. Using behavioural change frameworks, we aim to provide insights into the factors influencing app adoption.

item.title: First responders' experiences and training needs at the scene of a suspected suicide in Ireland: A mixed methods study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: First responders are categorised as those who are the first to respond to emergency calls and attend the site of an emergency. They include, but are not limited to police, emergency medical technicians, firefighters, and water safety personnel. First responders play a critical role in suicide postvention, supporting those bereaved by suicide and preventing adverse outcomes. However, many responders feel uncertain about how to effectively support those bereaved by suicide and often lack formal postvention training.

item.title: Comparison of Clinical Indicators for Differentiating Unipolar and Bipolar Depression.
item.description: BACKGROUND: The global prevalence of major depressive disorder and bipolar depression (BD) has increased, with BD often underdiagnosed and mismanaged. This study aims to identify key biomarkers from demographic and laboratory indicators to differentiate unipolar depression (UD) from BD, aiding early diagnosis and personalized treatment. METHODS: This study was conducted at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Xinxiang Medical University between January 2022 and December 2024. A total of 174 inpatients were included, with 87 diagnosed with UD and 87 with BD.

item.title: Clinical Symptomatology as Predictors of Early Treatment Response in Adolescents and Young Adults With Major Depressive Episode.
item.description: BACKGROUND: In clinics, major depressive episodes (MDE) in adolescents and early adults with mood disorders are a prevalent manifestation with limited treatment efficacy. Previous studies have suggested that early-stage treatment response is an important predictor of patients' final clinical outcome. Finding clinical features related to early-stage treatment response is crucial for optimizing interventions and understanding outcome determinants. METHODS: We conducted a study involving 218 inpatients aged 13-25 years with mood disorders currently in MDE.

item.title: "The war within": psychological mediators of the relationship between cumulative stress exposure and self-reported changes in gynecological symptoms among women during wartime.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Previous studies have tied stress exposure and psychological response, including posttraumatic stress symptoms (PTSS), to changes in gynecological symptoms (pain, urogenital symptoms and menstruation), however the multipartite relationship between these variables has been underexplored. METHODS: An online, cross sectional, survey was completed by 527 Israeli women during Israel-Gaza war. The questionnaires included demographics, gynecological symptoms before and after war onset, and validated scales for exposure to war-related stressors, exposure impact and PTSS.

item.title: [Not Available].
item.description: El trastorno de excoriación (TE), recientemente reconocido como entidad diagnóstica en el DSM-5, se caracteriza por conductas recurrentes de rascado compulsivo que generan lesiones cutáneas y un alto impacto emocional, funcional y social. Esta revisión integral aborda su fisiopatología, manifestaciones clínicas, comorbilidades y tratamiento, enfatizando la importancia de un abordaje multidisciplinario.

item.title: Health outcomes of U.S. active component service members working in high risk occupations for blast overpressure exposure: a retrospective cohort study.
item.description: Active component military service members are exposed to increased risk of occupational blast overpressure (BOP) exposure during deployment as well as training. This retrospective cohort study examined the incidence of first-time diagnoses of traumatic brain injury (TBI), insomnia, migraine headache, depressive or anxiety disorders, noise-induced hearing injury (NIHI), and essential hypertension among active component service members (ACSMs) in the U.S. Army, Air Force, and Marine Corps.

item.title: Reduced dorsal CA1 activity limits retention of the temporal component of declarative memory in the Cntnap2 knockout mouse model of autism.
item.description: Growing evidence implicates the hippocampus in the pathophysiology of autism spectrum disorder, particularly in the domains of social interactions and cognition. Yet, the mechanisms driving the hippocampal-dependent cognitive atypicalities in autism remain poorly defined. Here, we characterized how dysfunction of the CA1 subfield of the dorsal hippocampus drives abnormalities in critical components of declarative memory. item.title: Expanding Clinical and Variant Spectrum of CBX1-Related Syndrome: Report of Three Novel Cases.
item.description: CBX1-related syndrome is characterized by developmental delay, hypotonia, autistic features, and mild dysmorphic features. This syndrome is caused by heterozygous missense variants in CBX1, which encodes heterochromatin protein 1 beta (HP1β). These variants are situated within the chromodomain of HP1β, a critical region that mediates the interaction between HP1β and trimethylated H3K9. While a prior study identified three individuals with pathogenic CBX1 variants, the variant and clinical spectrum of CBX1-related syndrome remain largely unknown.

item.title: Identifying Potential Drug Targets for Treating ADHD From a Genetic Perspective: A Mendelian Randomization Study.
item.description: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a chronic neurodevelopmental disorder. Current pharmacological treatments have limitations, highlighting the need for new therapeutic targets. Using two-sample Mendelian randomization with cis-expression quantitative trait loci from the eQTLGen Consortium (31,684 individuals), we performed genomewide analysis against ADHD genomewide association study summary statistics from European ancestry (20,183 cases; 35,191 controls) and FinnGen R10 (2,788 cases; 405,153 controls).

item.title: Temporal predictability enhances response inhibition in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
item.description: OBJECTIVES: Individuals with ADHD have difficulty providing precise estimates of time. Nevertheless, they may still be able to harness temporally predictable information to guide behavior and regulate action control. We therefore examined whether temporal cueing improves impulse control or, conversely, exacerbates impulsive tendencies, in adults with ADHD. METHODS: Adults with ADHD and matched controls performed a temporally cued Simon task. Target onset time was either predictable or unpredictable, and lateralized responses were either compatible or incompatible with target location.

item.title: Feasibility and Safety of Transcranial Focused Ultrasound on Language Impairment in a Patient with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Case Report.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is defined by persistent difficulties with social communication and language, and a subset of children stay minimally verbal despite intensive interventions. The left amygdala and ventral-anterior superior temporal sulcus (STSva) form a key circuit for social-language integration, but how transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) might modulate in minimally verbal ASD has not been explored. CASE PRESENTATION: An 11-year-old minimally verbal ASD boy received 4 weeks of sequential tFUS stimulation (0.5 MHz).

item.title: Family socioeconomic status and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptoms in preschool children: a cross-sectional study of 21,366 parent-child dyads in Yan'an, western China.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Socioeconomic status (SES) is a well-established determinant of child mental health, yet evidence from large preschool populations in western China remains scarce. This study examined the association between family SES and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms in preschool children. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional survey among 21,366 parent-child dyads recruited from 189 public kindergartens in a western Chinese city using stratified cluster sampling.

item.title: Impact of a National Stepped-Care Model of Opioid Use Disorder Treatment on Access to Medication Therapies Among Homeless-Experienced Veterans.
item.description: OBJECTIVE: To determine whether the Veterans Health Administration's (VHA) Stepped Care for Opioid Use Disorder Train-the-Trainer (SCOUTT) initiative increased medication treatment for opioid use disorder (MOUD) among persons experiencing homelessness (PEH). STUDY SETTING AND DESIGN: We conducted a national retrospective cohort study of MOUD, including buprenorphine, naltrexone, or methadone, in federal fiscal years (FY) 2016-2020.

item.title: Is increased inflammation in schizophrenia associated with increased cardiovascular risk and the etiopathogenesis of this disorder?
item.description: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to examine the relationship between increased cardiovascular risk in schizophrenia and immune-inflammatory markers, including toll-like receptor (TLR)-2, TLR-4, and human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DR expression on monocytes and their subsets, and to investigate the associations between the QRISK3 score and inflammatory markers.

item.title: Post-Stroke Depression and Determinants in Ethiopia; A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined the prevalence and determinants of post-stroke depression (PSD) in Ethiopia, a low-resource setting where PSD remains understudied. The review included eight studies to quantify prevalence and identify risk factors, addressing a gap in global mental health disparities.
FINDINGS: The pooled prevalence of PSD in Ethiopia was 40.9% (95% CI: 26.52–55.28, p < 0.001), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 91.1%). Female sex (OR 3.51, 95% CI: 1.87–6.58), illiteracy (OR 2.02, 95% CI: 1.29–3.17), and age over 40 years (OR 1.59, 95% CI: 1.09–2.32) were significantly associated with higher odds of PSD.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is limited by high heterogeneity and a small number of included studies (n=8), which may affect the reliability of pooled estimates. The associations identified are plausible but should be interpreted cautiously due to potential unmeasured confounders (e.g., stroke severity, socioeconomic status). The lack of standardized screening tools across studies further limits comparability. While the prevalence is high, the clinical significance of these determinants needs validation in prospective cohorts.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians in Ethiopia and similar settings should screen for PSD, particularly in women, older patients, and those with low literacy. However, due to methodological limitations, these findings should prompt local quality improvement initiatives rather than definitive practice changes. Further research with standardized assessments is needed to confirm causality and inform targeted interventions.

item.title: Medical cannabis for the treatment of insomnia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This Cochrane systematic review assessed the benefits and harms of medical cannabis for adults with insomnia, synthesizing evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to inform clinical practice and policy. The review included nine studies (n=537) comparing medical cannabis with placebo or active comparators, focusing on sleep quality, total sleep time, adverse events, and other sleep-related outcomes.
FINDINGS: Compared with placebo, medical cannabis showed little to no clinically meaningful effect on sleep quality/satisfaction (SMD -0.49, 95% CI -1.06 to 0.08; 7 studies, 374 participants; very low-certainty evidence), total sleep time (MD 7.68 minutes, 95% CI -23.04 to 38.39; 6 studies, 194 participants; very low-certainty evidence), or daytime functioning (SMD -0.34, 95% CI -0.83 to 0.16; 5 studies, 144 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Quality of life showed a trend toward improvement (SMD 0.84, 95% CI -0.61 to 2.29; 3 studies, 95 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Adverse events were slightly more frequent with medical cannabis (OR 11.25, 95% CI 4.46 to 28.35; 3 studies, 98 participants; low-certainty evidence), though the absolute risk difference was not reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is very uncertain due to high risk of bias, serious inconsistency (I² up to 91%), and imprecision in effect estimates. The small sample sizes and heterogeneity in formulations (e.g., plant-based vs. synthetic cannabinoids) limit generalizability. While adverse events were more common with medical cannabis, the clinical significance is unclear due to low certainty. The review highlights the need for larger, well-designed RCTs with standardized outcomes and longer follow-up to clarify efficacy and safety.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support medical cannabis as an effective treatment for insomnia. Clinicians should exercise caution given the uncertain benefits and potential for adverse events. Further research is needed before considering medical cannabis for insomnia in routine practice.

item.title: Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Gender-Diverse Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA 2020) investigated how autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and autistic traits are assessed in gender-diverse populations, addressing a gap in diagnostic practices for this group.
FINDINGS: Of 28 included studies, only 6 (33%) used robust diagnostic criteria (e.g., DSM-5/ADOS), identifying 100 confirmed ASD cases among 1,855 participants (5.4%). The pooled prevalence of robust ASD diagnosis was 12% (95% CI: 7%-19%), while broader autism phenotype prevalence was 24% (95% CI: 17%-33%). Most studies relied on self-report or screening tools rather than standardized assessments.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests elevated ASD prevalence in gender-diverse groups, but methodological variability (e.g., reliance on non-diagnostic tools) and high risk of bias (per Joanna Briggs Institute tools) limit confidence. The pooled estimates may overstate true prevalence due to heterogeneity and lack of standardized diagnostic procedures. Training in ASD and gender diversity is needed to improve diagnostic accuracy.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice often lacks rigorous ASD assessment in gender-diverse patients. Clinicians should prioritize standardized diagnostic tools (e.g., ADOS-2, DSM-5 criteria) and be cautious interpreting self-report or screening results until more robust evidence emerges.

item.title: Education and training interventions for healthcare workers to prevent sexual harassment.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This Cochrane systematic review evaluated whether education or training interventions for healthcare workers reduce sexual harassment or improve knowledge/skills in managing it. It included only two small RCTs (170 nurses) comparing one type of harassment training against another, with no studies versus no intervention.
FINDINGS: Moderate-certainty evidence showed a small increase in “sexual harassment prevention” knowledge (MD 4.74 points on an unspecified scale, 95 % CI 1.21–8.28; 2 RCTs, 168 participants). Low-certainty evidence suggested possible small gains in “prevention strategy” (MD 11.70, 95 % CI 2.56–20.85) but not in “coping behaviour” (MD 6.36, 95 % CI –6.84 to 19.56). No study measured harassment incidence, mental health outcomes, sick leave, turnover, or organisational climate.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is extremely limited (two small Taiwanese nurse trials) and provides no direct evidence that training reduces harassment or improves mental health. Effect sizes are small and imprecise, and the GRADE rating is moderate to low. Risk of bias was judged low, but imprecision and indirectness (only nurses, only versus another training) limit external validity. Adverse effects and long-term outcomes were not assessed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data do not justify widespread implementation of sexual-harassment training as a preventive strategy in routine psychiatric care. Any adoption should be cautious, time-limited, and accompanied by rigorous outcome evaluation.

item.title: [Clinical evidence of acupuncture and moxibustion for depressive disorder: controversy, reflection and prospect].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the clinical evidence for acupuncture and moxibustion in treating depressive disorder, focusing on guidelines, systematic reviews, and trials to assess integration into mainstream psychiatric care. It highlights deficiencies and proposes directions for future research.
FINDINGS: The review identifies inconsistent recommendations across guidelines, methodological limitations in trials (e.g., small sample sizes, heterogeneity in techniques), and gaps in efficacy evaluation. Key issues include lack of standardized protocols, unclear mechanisms, and poor integration of mechanistic research with clinical practice.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak due to design flaws, heterogeneity, and limited high-quality trials. While the review suggests potential benefits, current data are insufficient to support routine use in psychiatric care. Strengths include a comprehensive critique of existing research; weaknesses stem from the narrative nature of the review and absence of quantitative synthesis.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Acupuncture/moxibustion for depression remains investigational. Clinicians should await robust RCTs before considering integration, and prioritize evidence-based treatments in routine care. Further research should address methodological rigor and standardization.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence in suicide prevention: promise, peril, and clinical implications for clinical practice.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) tools across the suicide prevention continuum, including risk detection, clinician training, and patient-facing psychotherapeutic support. It synthesizes early evidence on AI’s promise and risks in psychiatry, focusing on suicidal ideation (SI) detection and clinical integration.
FINDINGS: The review highlights studies suggesting AI models may detect SI more sensitively than clinicians by analyzing linguistic patterns, with reported improvements in clinician confidence and accuracy when AI is used adjunctively in risk assessments. AI-based virtual patients are cited as enhancing training outcomes, while CBT-inspired AI tools offer scalable support. However, most patient-facing AI tools remain unregulated and clinically unvalidated, raising concerns about safety and efficacy.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review without systematic methods or quantitative synthesis, this paper provides a conceptual overview rather than definitive evidence. The claims rely on selected studies without clear effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values, limiting the strength of conclusions. While the potential of AI is intriguing, the lack of rigorous validation and regulatory oversight underscores a critical gap between promise and clinical reality. The review appropriately flags ethical and safety risks but does not quantify harms or benefits.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current AI tools for suicide prevention should not replace standard clinical practice due to unproven efficacy and regulatory gaps. Clinicians should be aware of patient use of unvalidated AI tools and advocate for evidence-based integration. Further high-quality research—particularly randomized trials and regulatory frameworks—is urgently needed before AI can be recommended in routine care.

item.title: On the research on youth mental health: A scientometric analysis across mental disorders.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scientometric analysis mapped global research trends on youth mental health across disorders from 1985 to 2025, aiming to identify evolving priorities and gaps in the evidence base for adolescents and young adults.
FINDINGS: The study included 65,684 publications, revealing shifting foci: prevalence/outcomes in the 1980s; assessment tools and pharmacotherapy in the 1990s–2000s; early intervention for psychosis, ADHD, eating disorders, and suicide in the 2010s; and global burden, access to care, and COVID-19 in the 2020s. Novel 2023–2025 trends included substance use, lifestyle psychiatry, and non-suicidal self-injury. Most research originated from Western countries, with underrepresentation of lived experience involvement, open science, implementation research, and social determinants.
INTERPRETATION: As a scientometric analysis, this study provides a high-level overview of research trajectories rather than causal evidence. Strengths include its comprehensive scope and temporal mapping, but limitations include reliance on bibliometric data (not quality assessment) and geographic skew toward Western settings. The findings highlight evolving priorities but do not quantify clinical effectiveness or guide specific interventions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study underscores the need for broader, more inclusive research agendas in youth mental health, particularly addressing understudied areas like lived experience leadership and social determinants, but does not directly inform bedside practice.

item.title: Reducing Caregiver Burden in First-Episode Psychosis: Effects of a Psychoeducational Pathway Led by an Advanced Practice Nurse-A Multicentre Stepped-Wedge Randomized Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Family caregivers of people with first-episode psychosis (FEP) often experience high psychological distress and lack structured support. This multicentre stepped-wedge randomized controlled trial (RCT) in France evaluates whether a psychoeducational pathway led by advanced practice nurses (APNs) reduces caregiver burden over 6 months.
FINDINGS: The trial included six FEP centres and compared the APN-led psychoeducational pathway (initial consultation, single-family BREF programme, and multifamily PEPs Aidant programme) against usual care. The primary outcome was change in caregiver burden (measured by the Zarit Burden Interview) from baseline to 6 months. Secondary outcomes included caregiver mood (HADS), self-efficacy, quality of life, and patient engagement and recovery perception. The trial followed SPIRIT guidelines and was registered (NCT07041463). Quantitative results are not provided in the abstract.
INTERPRETATION: The stepped-wedge RCT design is appropriate for evaluating complex interventions in real-world settings, but the abstract lacks key quantitative results (effect sizes, confidence intervals, p-values, sample size, dropout). Without these, the magnitude and clinical significance of any observed reduction in caregiver burden remain unclear. The qualitative component will provide insight into implementation processes but does not address efficacy. The study’s external validity may be limited to French FEP services with APN capacity, and generalisability to other healthcare systems is uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This trial could inform the development of structured caregiver support pathways in FEP services, particularly if APNs are available. However, without published results, no changes to current practice can be recommended yet. Clinicians should await the full publication for effect sizes and feasibility data before considering adoption.

item.title: The effect of psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing on schizophrenia-related knowledge and hope among individuals with schizophrenia: A single-blind randomized controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This single-blind RCT (n=44) in a Turkish Community Mental Health Center tested whether adding psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing to routine care improves schizophrenia-related knowledge and hope compared with routine care alone in adults with schizophrenia.
FINDINGS: At baseline, groups were balanced (p > .05). Post-intervention, the intervention group showed large gains in knowledge (F = 176.060, p < .001, η² = 0.898) and hope (F = 99.782, p < .001, η² = 0.833), which persisted at one-month follow-up.
INTERPRETATION: The very large effect sizes and statistical significance suggest a robust short-term impact, but the single-centre design, small sample, and lack of assessor blinding raise risks of performance and detection bias. The follow-up is only one month, so durability beyond this horizon is unknown. Funding sources were not reported, so industry or academic bias cannot be excluded.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing may modestly boost insight and hope, but current evidence is preliminary; centres should pilot the programme while monitoring longer-term outcomes and adherence before widespread adoption.

item.title: The effect of tele-nursing counseling on functioning and medication adherence in individuals with bipolar disorder: A randomized controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) in a Swedish Community Mental Health Center (CMHC) tested whether structured tele-nursing counseling (weekly telephone calls plus supportive text messages for 8 weeks) improves functioning and medication adherence in 70 adults with bipolar disorder compared with usual care.
FINDINGS: After 8 weeks, the intervention group showed a mean improvement in FAST score of 6.8 points better than controls (95 % CI –9.8 to –3.7; p < 0.001) and a 2.11-point greater increase in MMAS adherence (95 % CI –2.4 to –1.8; p < 0.001), both adjusted for baseline values.
INTERPRETATION: The trial is small (n = 70) and of short duration (8 weeks), with no long-term follow-up or blinding of assessors. The effect sizes (≈7 FAST points; ≈2 MMAS points) are statistically significant but of uncertain clinical magnitude; minimal clinically important differences for FAST and MMAS are not established in this population. The study was retrospectively registered, raising minor concerns about outcome-reporting bias. Overall, the evidence is suggestive but preliminary.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Tele-nursing counseling may modestly improve short-term functioning and adherence in bipolar disorder, but larger, longer, and independently registered trials are needed before recommending routine adoption.

item.title: Development of a messenger RNA therapy for schizophrenia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical study explores whether a gene-targeted mRNA therapy could address a mechanistic gap in schizophrenia treatment, focusing on rare protein-truncating variants (PTVs) in the GRIA3 gene encoding the GluA3 subunit of the AMPA-type glutamate receptor. The study integrates population-based genetic screening, family-based validation, and animal modeling to justify a potential therapeutic approach.
FINDINGS: In a U.S. healthcare system cohort of 30,813 schizophrenia patients, two female relatives carried a rare PTV in GRIA3. Family analysis suggested an X-linked inheritance pattern linking the PTV to severe mental illness. Correction of the PTV in patient-derived neurons restored GRIA3 expression. An mRNA drug targeting GRIA3 was developed and tested in mice, showing good tolerability, broad brain expression of GluA3, and reversal of MK-801–induced behavioral abnormalities (a pharmacological psychosis model).
INTERPRETATION: This is a proof-of-concept study combining genetic discovery, cellular validation, and animal efficacy data. While the findings are promising—especially the functional rescue of neuronal deficits and behavioral abnormalities—they are preliminary and far removed from clinical application. The study is limited by its reliance on a single family, lack of human data, and use of a non-disease–specific animal model. The translational path to human trials will require addressing safety, delivery, and efficacy in more clinically relevant models.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this research does not change clinical practice but signals a potential future gene-targeted therapeutic avenue for a subset of patients with rare GRIA3 variants. Clinicians should be aware of emerging precision medicine approaches in psychiatry but should not expect immediate impact on treatment decisions.

item.title: Exploring the feasibility, safety and preliminary clinical effects of amygdala-targeted temporal interference stimulation for major depressive disorder: a pilot study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Temporal interference stimulation (TIS) is a novel noninvasive neuromodulation technique. However, whether it can be applied in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) remains unclear. This pilot study investigated the feasibility, safety, and preliminary clinical effects of amygdala-targeted TIS in patients with MDD. METHODS: In this single-center, single-arm pilot study, 32 MDD patients received a 5-day amygdala-targeted TIS.

item.title: Differential changes in frontolimbic functional connectivity following 12-week psychostimulant monotherapy in ADHD youth with and without familial risk for bipolar I disorder.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Although attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), psychostimulant medications, and BD family history are risk factors for developing bipolar I disorder (BD), their contribution to the aberrant ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC) and amygdala (AMY) functional connectivity (FC) implicated in the pathophysiology of BD remain unclear.

item.title: The relationship between physical activity and mental health in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): A scoping review.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are at risk of developing secondary mental health problems. Physical activity (PA) has recently gained attention as a non-pharmacological intervention. However, studies that comprehensively organize its effects on different aspects of mental health remain limited. This study aimed to systematically organize existing evidence on the effects of PA on the mental health of children with ADHD. METHODS: This scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines.

item.title: Pain-contingent opioid use and addiction risk in cancer pain: a reappraisal of around-the-clock dosing.
item.description: Around-the-clock (ATC) opioid dosing has anchored cancer pain management since an era of advanced disease, continuous pain, and short survival, when undertreatment was the dominant clinical failure. Contemporary oncology increasingly involves prolonged survival and chronic treatment-related pain, and advances in behavioral pharmacology and addiction neuroscience challenge the assumption that dosing schedules are behaviorally neutral.

item.title: Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcome Following Three Randomized Controlled Trials of Choline in Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD).
item.description: BACKGROUND: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) represents a range of neurodevelopmental outcomes from prenatal alcohol exposure for which there are few interventions. Preclinical studies have identified choline as a potential treatment for cognitive deficits in FASD. We previously conducted three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in children under age 6 and reported on memory benefits following all three trials. Two RCTs compared a fixed 500 mg daily dose to placebo, and the third RCT tested a weight-adjusted choline dose.

item.title: Excitation-Inhibition Balance and Fronto-Limbic Connectivity Distinguish TMS Treatment Outcomes in Refractory Depression.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is effective for treatment-resistant depression, but outcomes remain variable. The neurophysiological mechanisms underlying response remain poorly understood, limiting precision neuromodulation. METHODS: We combined transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and connectome-based Jansen-Rit neural mass modeling to investigate the mechanistic basis of treatment efficacy in 90 patients with treatment-resistant depression.

item.title: Comparing family history indicators and polygenic scores in depressive disorder.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Genetic liability of depressive disorder can be captured by psychopathology in relatives (family history). Various methods summarize family history in a single score, differing in included information as well as the underlying model. We systematically compared the performance of family history indicators, including promising new indicators based on the liability threshold model, in predicting depressive disorder.
